source_read: PDF, pp. 1–7 (all pages; Tables 1–3 checked on rendered p. 4)

claims.overstatement: None in the Green sentence itself. The claim's opening frame (single analogues dissolved in water, compared with known content) does not describe Green's four samples, which were police-seized material whose content came from forensic GC/MS, one with heroin and one a counterfeit pill ground to powder; four samples only (editors' Wilson 95% CI for 4/4: 51.0–100%).
claims.note: Recomputed 4/4. The strip maker's list of analogues the strip detects (relayed on p. 2) includes carfentanil, remifentanil and sufentanil; this is the maker's statement, not tested by Green.

anchors.extracted: Four seized samples were eligible: acetyl fentanyl alone (n = 2), furanyl fentanyl alone (n = 1), furanyl fentanyl with heroin (n = 1). The fentanyl strip (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive on all four (4/4). One was a counterfeit pill containing furanyl fentanyl, which Raman and FTIR missed.

anchors.locator: Methods › Sensitivity and specificity procedures, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Exploratory subset: police samples (n = 4) containing any fentanyl analogue alone or with drugs other than fentanyl were eligible; identities from the earlier forensic GC/MS; not prepared solutions of known concentration.

Per the maker, the strip indicates fentanyl and the analogues norfentanyl, acetyl fentanyl, carfentanil, furanyl fentanyl, butyryl fentanyl, valeryl fentanyl, ocfentanil, 3-methyl fentanyl, remifentanil, sufentanil and p-fluorofentanyl (maker's claim, not tested in this study).

claims.overstatement: None for Green's numbers. Two conditions could be stated more fully: (1) because the reference GC/MS detected fentanyl only from 3.1 or 100 µg/mL, the positive group can hold only samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS, so sensitivity for samples with little fentanyl may be lower than 98%; (2) the limit-of-detection solutions were described as prepared in ethanol (p. 3), and the diluent used for the strips is not stated, so 'pure fentanyl solutions' is not necessarily water.
claims.note: Recomputed: 52/52 = 100.0%, 52/54 = 96.3%, pooled 104/106 = 98.1%, Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5% (same as the claim). Per laboratory, Wilson 93.1–100% and 87.5–99.0%. 100–150 ng/mL = Table 1's 0.100–0.150 mcg/mL. The abstract's false-negative 3.7% is the Rhode Island value, not the pooled 1.9%.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (fentanyl-positive rows) and Table 3 (fentanyl test strips, sensitivity)
anchors.extracted: Fentanyl-positive by earlier GC/MS: 52 Baltimore, 54 Providence (fentanyl alone 29 and 35). Strip sensitivity 100.0% (Baltimore, 52/52) and 96.3% (Rhode Island, 52/54); pooled 104/106 = 98.1% (editors' Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%).
Text gives 100% in Baltimore and 96% in Providence; the two missed fentanyl samples contained fentanyl only.

anchors.locator: Table 1 and Results › Limit of detection, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Lowest concentration detected by the strip: 0.150 mcg/mL (Baltimore) and 0.100 mcg/mL (Rhode Island), i.e. 100–150 ng/mL; GC/MS limits 100 mcg/mL (Baltimore) and 3.1 mcg/mL (Rhode Island); Raman 25 mcg/mL; FTIR 3–4% by weight.

anchors.locator: Methods › Limits of detection procedures, 1st–2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Fentanyl standards from DEA-registered vendors prepared in ethanol solutions; triplicate tests at serially lower concentrations, then 25% steps; 7 further replicates at the estimated limit; an unclear or indeterminate reading counted as not detected.

anchors.locator: Methods › Sensitivity and specificity procedures, 1st–2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: 106 fentanyl-positive and 104 fentanyl-negative police samples of personal quantities (exhibits of 1 g or less, small-scale distribution) chosen on earlier GC/MS results by people not involved in testing; strips used per package insert by chemists blinded to content after a 30-minute training; samples dissolved in tap water (Baltimore) or deionized water (Providence); testing in September–October 2017 (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 2).

All samples were tested as powders (pills ground); between-laboratory differences in strip performance possibly due to the different GC/MS detection limits, undetected analogues or other factors (authors' hypothesis).

claims.overstatement: None. 'Some may have held traces of fentanyl' is an editors' inference from Table 1; the authors' own hypothesis (p. 5) names different GC/MS limits and undetected fentanyl analogues as possible reasons for the laboratory difference, so 'traces of fentanyl or of an analogue' would match the source more closely.
claims.note: Recomputed: 51/52 = 98.1%, 47/52 = 90.4%, pooled 98/104 = 94.2%, Wilson 95% CI 88.0–97.3% (same as the claim); false positives 6/104 = 5.8% (Wilson 2.7–12.0%). The five described false positives are all from Providence (methamphetamine and noscapine samples occur only in the Providence negatives, Table 2); the Baltimore one is not described. The abstract's 9.6% false-positive rate is the Rhode Island value, and the Discussion (6th paragraph, p. 5) swaps the two rates (9.6% false negative, 3.7% false positive).

anchors.locator: Table 2 (fentanyl-negative rows) and Table 3 (fentanyl test strips, specificity)
anchors.extracted: Fentanyl-negative by earlier GC/MS: 52 Baltimore, 52 Providence (mostly cocaine, heroin, oxycodone, benzodiazepines; methamphetamine 3 and noscapine 1 in Providence only). Specificity 98.1% (51/52) and 90.4% (47/52); pooled 98/104 = 94.2% (editors' Wilson 88.0–97.3%); 6 false positives.
The five samples read falsely positive contained by GC/MS buprenorphine only (1), heroin only (2), methamphetamine only (1) and noscapine only (1).

Reference GC/MS limits 100 mcg/mL (Baltimore) and 3.1 mcg/mL (Rhode Island), against 0.150 and 0.100 mcg/mL for the strip: the reference cannot rule out small amounts of fentanyl in 'negative' samples.
Authors attribute the small laboratory differences in strip sensitivity and specificity possibly to GC/MS detection limits, undetected fentanyl analogues or other factors.

Abstract reports false negative 3.7% and false positive 9.6% (the Rhode Island figures, not pooled); the Discussion states at most 9.6% false negative and at most 3.7% false positive, the reverse of Table 3.

claims.overstatement: None; the claim presents it as how the strips are built. These are the authors' and maker's descriptions, not tested findings.

anchors.extracted: The strips do not measure fentanyl concentration, do not distinguish fentanyl from any of the analogues and show presence only; approved in Canada (not the US) for urine, so drug checking is off-label.
Authors: the strips give no other information on quantity, purity, adulterants or fill.

key_findings.correction: Content confirmed, but the page range should be 1–4: Table 2 (and the Table 3 header giving N = 104 Baltimore, N = 106 Rhode Island) is on p. 4, not pp. 1–3.
Also found in step 1: the five described match Providence, where the only methamphetamine and noscapine negatives are (Table 2).
83.3% fits 45/54; 90.2% fits 46/51 and no fraction of 52, as the note says.
The maker's list has 11 names, one of them the metabolite norfentanyl.
Note: the paragraph on mixtures and pills concerns identification by the spectrometers (library matching), not the strip, and the Raman between-laboratory explanation is offered as one hypothesis.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in step 1; pooled 2/106 = 1.9% and 6/104 = 5.8%.
Checked: 91.5% and 90.2% cannot be formed from 52, whereas the other Table 3 percentages fit 52 or 54 (e.g. Raman 2/52 and 2/54, SERS 20/52, 33/54 and 48/52).

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high: agree, as I do with sample selection high, reference standard high and flow and timing unclear. Single-domain difference: index test I would rate low rather than unclear. Readers were blind to content and used the package-insert rule, so both QUADAS-2 signalling questions are yes; the unreported amount dissolved, water volume, lot and faint-line handling are better recorded as applicability concerns. The reasoning calls sensitivity 'in these samples' robust. I would add the mirror image of the specificity problem: the reference detected fentanyl only from 3.1 or 100 mcg/mL, so the positive group can hold only samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS, and sensitivity for samples with little fentanyl may be lower (spectrum effect).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The card's points are right; 'available and valid' also covers a Raman device with 3.7–61% sensitivity, although the abstract does call the other devices less sensitive.

missed: The limit-of-detection standards were prepared in ethanol (p. 3), and the diluent used for the strips is not stated. Organic solvents can affect these strips (sc_sisco_2024b, solvent side study), so the 100–150 ng/mL limits may not carry over to water.
Sensitivity is likely overstated for samples with little fentanyl, because the reference standard set the bar for entering the positive group (see risk_of_bias note).

The replication timeline treats Bergh et al. (2021) and Lockwood et al. (2021) as known only through Sisco et al. (2024b) and not read, but both are read in this round (sc_bergh_2021 is in the same file); the timeline and where_it_stands could be updated.
